# loading libraries
```{r}
library(xgboost)
library(rio)
library(caret)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(rio)
library(pROC)
```


## LOAD DATA SET
```{r}
health_data<- read.csv("diabetes.csv")
head(health_data)
```
# check for missing values
```{r}
health_data<-na.omit(health_data)
colSums((is.na(health_data)))
```



# confirm for missing values
```{r}
colSums((is.na(health_data)))
```

# structure
```{r}
str(health_data)
table(health_data$diabetes)
```


### convert categorical variables into factor
```{r}
health_data$diabetes<-as.factor(health_data$diabetes)
```


## split thye data set
```{r}
set.seed(123)
trainIndexed<- createDataPartition(
  health_data$diabetes,
  p=0.8, list=FALSE
)
train<-health_data[trainIndexed, ]
test<- health_data[- trainIndexed, ]
```


## one hot encoding variables
```{r}
dummy<-dummyVars(diabetes~., data=train)
train_x<-predict(dummy, train)
test_x<-predict(dummy, test)
train_y<-as.numeric(as.character(train$diabetes))
test_y<-as.numeric(as.character(test$diabetes))
```


# create dmatrix
```{r}
dtrain<-xgb.DMatrix(
  data=train_x,
  label=train_y
)
dtest<-xgb.DMatrix(
  data=test_x,
  label=test_y
)
```


# train xgboost model
```{r}
params<-list(
  objective="binary:logistic",
  eval_metric="logloss",
  max_depth=4, eta=0.10,
  subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8
)
xgb_model<-xgb.train(params=params, data=dtrain, nrounds=100,
                     watchlist=list(train=dtrain), verbose=1)
```

### make predictions
```{r}
make_predictions<-predict(
  xgb_model, dtest
)
predictions<-ifelse(
  make_predictions>0.5,
  1,
  0
)
```


# confusion matrix
```{r}
confusionMatrix(
  factor(predictions),
  factor(test_y)
)
```
- The Confusion Matrix (The Raw Numbers)A confusion matrix compares what the model predicted against the actual reference truth. 
The dataset has 219 total samples, split by the model like this:
True Positives (122): 
The actual class was 0, and the model correctly predicted 0.
True Negatives (95): The actual class was 1, 
and the model correctly predicted 1.False Positives (2):
The actual class was 1, but the model incorrectly guessed 0.False Negatives (0): The actual class was 0, and the model never missed it.
- Overall Model Performance MetricsThese metrics evaluate how well the model works as a whole across all data points: Accuracy (99.09%): The overall success rate. The model guessed correctly 217 out of 219 times. 95% Confidence Interval (96.74%, 99.89%): A statistical range. If you ran this model on new, identical distributions of data, you can be 95% confident the accuracy would fall between these two percentages. No Information Rate / NIR (55.71%): The accuracy you would get by blindly guessing the majority class (Class 0) every single time. P-Value [Acc > NIR] (< 2e-16): A measure of statistical significance. Because it is essentially zero, it proves your model’s high accuracy is due to genuine predictive power, not random luck. Kappa (0.9815): Measures agreement between predictions and reality, adjusted for chance. A score above 0.80 is considered excellent; 0.98 indicates near-perfect reliability. McNemar's Test P-Value (0.4795): Checks if the model's errors are heavily biased toward one type of mistake over another. A high p-value (greater than 0.05) means your small number of misclassifications (just 2 errors) are statistically balanced.
- Class-Specific Metrics (Class 0 as 'Positive')Because Class 0 is designated as the target "Positive" class, the performance breaks down into specific dimensions of accuracy: Sensitivity / Recall (100.00%): Out of all actual Class 0 cases in the data, the model found every single one. It missed zero positive cases.Specificity (97.94%): Out of all actual Class 1 cases, the model correctly identified 97.94% of them. It only misclassified two.Balanced Accuracy (98.97%): The average of Sensitivity and Specificity. It gives an honest view of performance when classes are unevenly split.Positive Predictive Value / Precision (98.39%): When the model claims a sample is Class 0, it is right 98.39% of the time.Negative Predictive Value (100.00%): When the model claims a sample is Class 1, it is right every single time.
-Data Split & PrevalencePrevalence (55.71%): The actual proportion of Class 0 in your entire dataset (\(122/219\)).Detection Rate (55.71%): The rate at which the model successfully found true positives relative to the total dataset size.Detection Prevalence (56.62%): The total proportion of the dataset that the model claimed belonged to Class 0, regardless of whether it was right or wrong (\(124/219\)).
- Formatting Styles ExplainedWhen putting this data into a final report, the writing changes drastically based on who is reading it: Academic / APA Style: Written for researchers, peer reviews, or journals. It relies heavily on parenthetical statistics, technical terminology, and exact numerical representations (e.g., “The classifier demonstrated a significant improvement over the baseline No Information Rate, χ²... p < .001...”). Business / Executive Style: Written for project stakeholders, managers, or clients. It strips away technical jargon (like Kappa or McNemar's) and frames the numbers around risk and operational reliability (e.g., “Our system operates at a 99.09% success rate. Crucially, it has a 0% fail-miss rate for Class 0, meaning no critical targets are bypassed...”). 

### ROC_CURVE
```{r}
roc_curve<-roc(
test_y,
make_predictions
)
plot(
roc_curve,
col="skyblue",
main="Roc Curve"
)

```
